summary: Acceptance-tested the /dashboard skeleton-flash fix end-to-end (page.tsx server component, new DashboardBody.tsx, deleted layout.tsx). AC-1 through AC-5 all PASS with independent spot-check evidence: (AC-1) clean-rebuilt the app myself and re-ran app/tests/components/dashboardBody.test.tsx in isolation (3/3 pass) confirming real DuelRecordCard content renders on first frame with authLoading=true and no SkeletonCard, then ran the full gate suite myself from that clean build (lint clean, typecheck clean, 81 files/748 tests pass). (AC-2) did my own from-scratch `rm -rf .next && pnpm build`, confirmed `ƒ /dashboard` in the route table and independently re-checked .next/prerender-manifest.json — /dashboard is absent from the static route list. (AC-3) curled /dashboard with no cookie -> 307 (unchanged presence-only proxy redirect); with a forged cookie -> 200, initialData:null, fallback chrome renders, no crash. (AC-4) minted my own forged-but-structurally-valid RS256 JWT (correct iss/aud/exp, attacker-chosen sub/email, garbage signature) independent of security-reviewer's own probe, hit a live `pnpm start` instance of this exact build: 200 response, zero occurrences of the forged uid/email anywhere in the HTML/RSC payload, Cache-Control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate. (AC-5) re-ran `git diff --stat` on all four protected files myself -- empty output, third independent confirmation after software-engineer and the two reviewers. HOWEVER: resolved the open staleness question (reviewer's finding #3, back/forward after a mutation) as REAL and REACHABLE, which per the task's explicit decision rule makes this an acceptance failure, not an acceptable non-blocking warning. Built two throwaway auth-free ƒ (dynamic) probe routes rendering Date.now(), ran `pnpm build && pnpm start` (this app's real production config, no staleTimes override, experimental:{}), and drove a real Chromium instance via Playwright: navigated probe-a -> probe-b via next/link (client-side nav, confirmed by differing timestamps) -> waited 1.5s (>> staleTimes.dynamic=0) -> browser Back button. Result: the restored probe-a page showed the IDENTICAL Date.now() from the first visit -- no fresh server request was made on back-navigation, despite the route being fully dynamic and staleTimes.dynamic=0. Corroborated this authoritatively by reading Next.js 16.3.4's own shipped source in node_modules: dispatchTraverseAction (fired on the popstate listener, app-router-instance.js) unconditionally dispatches ACTION_RESTORE, which router-reducer.js routes unconditionally to restoreReducer.js -> startPPRNavigation(..., FreshnessPolicy.HistoryTraversal, ...) -> ppr-navigations.js's createCacheNodeForSegment 'case 2' (HistoryTraversal) calls segment-cache/bfcache.js's readFromBFCache, which explicitly passes -1 instead of the real clock time to bypass staleness checks, with the Next.js team's own inline comment: 'During a back/forward navigation, it doesn't matter how stale the data might be' and 'A back/forward navigation will disregard the stale time.' This is a structurally distinct freshness-policy branch from 'case 0' (Default, used by regular Link/router.push navigation via navigate-reducer.js), which DOES call the time-respecting readFromBFCacheDuringRegularNavigation and DOES honor staleTimes.dynamic=0 -- so the prior cycle's staleTimes.dynamic=0 conclusion was correct for that path and does NOT generalize to back/forward, exactly as this task's brief hypothesized. Also checked whether Next 16's newer Activity-style full-component-state preservation (bfcache-state-manager.js, useRouterBFCache) would instead make DashboardBody's live instance persist rather than remount: MAX_BF_CACHE_ENTRIES = process.env.__NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS ? 3 : 1, and this repo's next.config.js does not enable cacheComponents, so only the single active tree is tracked -- DashboardBody genuinely unmounts/remounts on navigation, fed by the stale segment-level BFCache entry described above (not a preserved live instance). This also explains why the OLD pre-fix code self-healed: its RSC segment carried no server-computed data to go stale (just a client-component reference), so its mount-effect fetchDashboard() reran fresh on every genuine remount, untouched by the segment cache. Applied to the task's concrete repro (dashboard with pre-duel record -> /duel -> win -> Back): the restored /dashboard CacheNode carries the pre-duel initialData prop with needsDynamicRequest:false (no fetch spawned), DashboardBody seeds fetchState from it, and the client fetch effect's `initialData !== null` guard permanently suppresses correction -- stale win/loss record with no self-heal path, exactly reviewer's predicted defect, now confirmed via both live browser reproduction and Next.js source. Not a trust-boundary/security defect (it's the user's own data, no cross-user exposure, consistent with the AC-4 findings), but it is a real, reachable behavioral regression against this change's own stated goal of preserving existing behavior, on the single most likely revisit flow a dashboard has. All probe routes/scripts deleted immediately after use; git status confirmed clean (only the four files under review remain in the diff) before writing this handoff. Full report at loop/qa-report.md.

findings.location: app/app/dashboard/DashboardBody.tsx:67-71,105-109 (interacting with Next.js 16.3.4's back/forward client router cache)
findings.issue: Confirmed reachable via live browser reproduction and Next.js 16.3.4 source reading (see summary): browser Back/forward navigation to /dashboard after the user has navigated away and their duel/climb stats changed server-side restores the previously-cached RSC payload -- including the stale server-resolved `initialData` prop -- without any fresh network request, because Next's history-traversal navigation path (`FreshnessPolicy.HistoryTraversal`) explicitly bypasses `staleTimes.dynamic` (confirmed by the Next.js team's own source comments). Because `DashboardBody`'s client fetch effect permanently early-returns once `initialData !== null`, there is no self-correction path. This is a regression versus the pre-fix behavior, whose client-side mount effect re-fetched fresh data on every remount regardless of any cached RSC segment. Violates this change's own stated goal of preserving all existing behavior.
findings.fix: Either sync the prop instead of only seeding it (`useEffect(() => { if (initialData) setFetchState({status:'success', data: initialData}); }, [initialData])`, which self-heals on any prop change including a bfcache-restored stale one only if Next re-invokes the server component -- verify this actually helps for the HistoryTraversal path specifically, since a bypassed fetch means the prop itself won't change either) or make the client fetch a post-paint background revalidate that runs unconditionally after first paint (drop the `initialData !== null` guard on the effect but keep the seeded state for zero-flash first paint). Recommend software-engineer verify the chosen fix against a real back-navigation repro (the probe-route method used here, or a real signed-in session) before declaring it resolved, not just against the FetchState seed logic in isolation.

findings.issue: Carried forward from reviewer's finding: two producers of DashboardData, only one (page.tsx) is type-checked against the shared interface; route.ts builds an untyped literal. They agree today but will silently diverge on a future field change, breaking only the client-fallback path.
findings.fix: Extract a shared `buildDashboardPayload(uid): Promise<DashboardData>` and call it from both page.tsx and route.ts, annotating the route's response so tsc checks it too. Bundle into the same revision pass as the staleness fix since software-engineer will already be in these files.

findings.issue: Carried forward from reviewer's finding: BetaBanner mounts ~100-500ms late on the server-populated path (gated on client-only `token`), causing a layout shift that didn't exist pre-fix, even though `betaJoined` is already known server-side and could drive this instead.
findings.fix: Use `fetchState.data.user.betaJoined` to drive the banner's visibility/space directly instead of `token &&`. Bundle into the same revision pass.

learnings.insight: Next.js 16.3.4's browser back/forward (popstate) navigation is handled by a structurally distinct code path from regular navigation, and it explicitly bypasses `staleTimes.dynamic` by design -- confirmed by the Next.js team's own inline comments in node_modules/next/dist/client/components/segment-cache/bfcache.js ('A back/forward navigation will disregard the stale time... only relevant when staleTimes.dynamic is enabled') and by a live Playwright/Chromium reproduction against two throwaway ƒ (dynamic) probe routes rendering Date.now(): identical timestamp restored after Back + 1.5s wait, despite staleTimes.dynamic=0. This directly falsifies any blanket claim that 'staleTimes.dynamic=0 means no client-side staleness can occur' -- that claim is only true for regular Link/router.push navigation (FreshnessPolicy.Default, navigate-reducer.js), not for history traversal (FreshnessPolicy.HistoryTraversal, restore-reducer.js). Any page using the settings/SettingsForm 'seed initialData once, suppress client fetch forever' pattern inherits this gap on any route whose underlying data can change from a flow the user might reach via Back (e.g. dashboard after a duel, any record/stat page after a mutating side-quest).
learnings.action: When a prior conclusion about Next.js router staleness is being reused for a new page, re-verify it specifically for the navigation type in question (regular vs. back/forward vs. server-action-refresh) rather than assuming it generalizes. For any future 'server-resolves-payload-then-hands-to-client-initialData' conversion, either add a real back-navigation-after-mutation step to acceptance testing before merge, or default to a background-revalidate-after-first-paint pattern instead of a permanent seed-and-suppress pattern.

learnings.insight: A cheap, auth-free way to empirically test Next.js's client router bfcache/staleness behavior for any given app's exact build/config: add two throwaway dynamic (ƒ) routes (e.g. via headers()/cookies()) that each render Date.now() and link to each other via next/link, `pnpm build && pnpm start`, then drive a real browser (Playwright, with executablePath pointed at whatever chromium binary is actually available in the sandbox if the default install/version doesn't match) through: visit A, click to B, wait past the configured staleTimes, browser Back, compare A's timestamp before/after. This isolates the router mechanism from the feature's own auth/data complexity and produces a definitive real-browser answer in a couple of minutes. Route folders prefixed with `_` (including `__`) are Next.js private folders excluded from routing -- use a plain alphanumeric name for throwaway probes or the build will silently produce nothing.
learnings.action: Reuse this probe pattern for any future 'is X actually reachable in the client router cache' question instead of relying solely on source-reading or assuming a general staleTimes rule applies uniformly across navigation types.

learnings.insight: `pnpm start`/`next dev` in this repo auto-generates app/AGENTS.md and app/CLAUDE.md (a Next.js 16 'agent rules' file, self-documented as written by `next dev`/`next start` and safe to delete -- it regenerates). It is untracked build noise, not a real change; delete before finishing if your own commands triggered it, same as the existing next-env.d.ts churn note from the software-engineer/verifier handoffs.
learnings.action: After any `pnpm start`/`pnpm dev` invocation during verification, check `git status --short` for AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/test-results alongside the already-known next-env.d.ts churn, and clean up before writing your handoff.
